19953-origin-and-development-of-form-and:
William H. Holmes traced the origin and development of form and ornament in ceramic art. Living tribes' art, he argues, can illuminate pre-Columbian art's obscure passages. Peoples least influenced by whites preserve the oldest methods best. Holmes supplements excavation with ethnology throughout the study. Potsherds become evidence of whole design systems here. The work appeared under the Bureau of Ethnology's imprint.

Holmes was a geologist, artist, and archaeologist in one career. His ceramic studies classified decoration by its growth from technique. Basket marks, coils, and tools explain painted designs in his theory. The argument shaped American archaeology for decades. His drawings alone make the volume valuable. It is a founding text of ceramic anthropology.
20301-a-museum-for-young-gentlemen-and-l:
A Museum for Young Gentlemen and Ladies is a private tutor for youth at home. It gathers facts on many subjects in one small, handy book. The original was tiny, about nine centimeters in size and scope. Each line held only eight or nine words on average there.

That small scale shaped the plain, packed style of the whole work. Such books taught manners, nature, trade, and morals before school was common. A museum, then, meant a storehouse of wonders, not a building alone. Young readers got a pocket tutor full of facts worth knowing.
20434-the-boy-scouts-first-camp-fire-or-:
The Boy Scouts' First Camp Fire, published in 1913, follows a troop of boys learning scouting with the Silver Fox patrol. Camp life, hikes, and tests of skill fill the chapters. The boys learn to watch, listen, and remember what they see.

One lesson comes straight from the instruction book. A true scout keeps his eyes and ears open to see and hear everything. The more a boy can recall from a store window after one minute's look, the higher he stands. Such drills, mixed with outdoor fun, made these books favorites with the first scouting generation.
21047-the-nursery-no-109-january-1876-vo:
Fine drawings in this number need no praise from us, The Nursery tells its readers for January 1876. Merrill's Christmas at the North and Sheppard's at the South earn warm words. Harrison Weir's two dogs are called capital work in the same breath.

The Nursery, a monthly magazine for the youngest readers, mixes tales, verse, and plates. Large print and short pieces suit children just past picture books alone. Volume nineteen's New Year number shows its cosy store at full charm. Such magazines taught generations of American children to love the printed page, one short, bright piece at a time.
22028-the-war-service-of-the-1-4-royal-b:
C. R. M. F. Cruttwell, a former captain in the battalion, wrote The War Service of the 1/4 Royal Berkshire Regiment at his old commanding officer's request. The history first ran in the Berkshire Chronicle in 1920, while the Great War was still fresh. Berkshire families then paid to see it reprinted as a book. Cruttwell follows a Territorial battalion of county men through the whole war.

Such regimental histories record marches, trenches, attacks, and the names of the fallen. This one was made for the men who served and the homes that lost them. Its value now lies in the detail only an insider could supply. It shows how one English county battalion endured the First World War.
22627-german-science-reader-an-introduct:
Charles F. Kroeh wrote the German Science Reader, a 1907 textbook introducing students of physics, chemistry, and engineering to scientific German. In Kroeh's day, German was a working language of science, and no researcher could thrive without reading it. His reader bridges language study and the laboratory.

His method is practical: translate a passage, then read the German again and again, aloud, with pauses and emphasis, as if telling the thoughts to another person. Pronouncing words and sentences, he argues, fixes them in memory. Graded readings in the sciences follow the advice. The book now serves language historians and any scientist who still meets older German literature in the stacks.
23107-a-book-of-discovery-the-history-of:
M. B. Synge marches through exploration history in A Book of Discovery. Her contents run like a drum roll. The Vikings sail the northern seas. The end of medieval exploration comes. Prince Henry of Portugal appears. Bartholomew Diaz reaches the stormy cape. Vasco da Gama reaches India. Balboa sees the Pacific. Magellan sails round the world. Cortes explores and conquers Mexico.

Synge wrote history for young readers with a storyteller's pace, and this survey covers the whole age of sail and discovery. Each chapter turns a voyage into a tale while keeping the map in view. The viewpoint is British and of its time, proud of the road from Diaz to the empire. As an introduction that generations actually finished, the book earned its long life.

further-adventures-of-quincy-adams-sawye: Charles Felton Pidgin's further adventures of Quincy Adams Sawyer and the Mason Corner folks — more New England humor, kindness, and heart. The beloved characters return for new escapades. A welcome sequel for all old friends of the book. Huldah's wit and Quincy's kindness shine as brightly as before.
history-of-the-catholic-church-from-the-: James MacCaffrey traces the Catholic Church from the Renaissance popes to the French Revolution. Reform, wars of creed, and the Church's trials fill a fair-minded narrative. A solid and readable church history. MacCaffrey's fairness won praise from all sides.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-f:
Part F completes the 1860 Virtue edition of David Hume's History of England, closing the sixth and final part. Hume's history, published from 1754 to 1762, ends with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, where its seventy-one chapters stop. The philosopher from Edinburgh had written the book his whole century read.

The final part brings the long contest of crown and parliament to its settlement. Hume's even hand and lucid style held readers who agreed with nothing else he wrote. For a hundred years, to know English history meant to have read Hume's version of it. Part F sets the last stone on that monument, and the set stands complete.
mary-schweidler-the-amber-witch-the-most:
Wilhelm Meinhold wrote The Amber Witch, in Lady Duff Gordon's English version. The title page calls it the most famed witch trial ever known. It claims to print a flawed old text by Mary's father.

Abraham Schweidler was pastor of Coserow, on the island of Usedom. In chapter seven, troops rob him and sack the church. His cow dies, food runs out, and troops burn half a nearby town. He flees with Mary and old Ilse to a cave in the woods. Starved children beg bread, and Mary shares what food is left. Want, war, and fear set the ground for the witch charge to come.
memorial-addresses-on-the-life-and-chara:
Memorial Addresses on William H. F. Lee were printed by Congress in 1892. The Government Printing Office in Washington made the book. Lee had served as a Representative from Virginia in Congress.

Speeches in the House and Senate make up the whole volume. Both chambers agreed in March 1892 to print eight thousand copies. Two thousand went to the Senate, and four thousand to the House. A portrait of Lee, engraved for the book, fronts the addresses. Fifty bound copies in morocco went to Lee's own family. The rest spread through both chambers for members and their state.
missionary-survey-as-an-aid-to-intellige:
Roland Allen and Thomas Cochrane published this study of mission planning in 1920. Allen, once an SPG missionary in North China, wrote the text. Cochrane, late principal of Union Medical College in Peking, studied the material with him. Their preface argues that missionary forces show little evidence of plan or method.

One region, they note, holds some 450 missionaries for three million people. Another, with twice the population, has only about twenty. Such gaps make survey, meaning systematic fact-finding, absolutely imperative. The book urges churches to distribute workers by knowledge rather than habit, so that cooperation in foreign missions becomes intelligent.
narrative-of-the-overland-expedition-of-:
Frederick J. Byerley compiled this tale from the Jardine brothers' journals. J. W. Buxton printed it in Brisbane in 1867. The brothers drove stock from Rockhampton to Cape York, in northern Queensland. Byerley worked as an engineer of roads in that district.

The book is inscribed to Sir Charles Nicholson of Sydney University. He is praised as an old, distinguished colonist. The Jardines crossed wild, unmapped country with cattle and horses. Rivers, hunger, and hostile encounters marked the long road north. Their trek opened Cape York to settlement, and this plain record, drawn from their own journals, keeps its grit.
nasa-tm-19660012971-extension-of-the-pho:
Norman F Ness at Goddard and John M Wilcox at the University of California, Berkeley, traced the Sun's surface magnetic field outward into space in this February 1965 paper. The photosphere is the Sun's visible surface, where the field is rooted. Magnetometer readings from the IMP-1 satellite measured the field near Earth. The authors compare those readings with observations of the Sun itself.

If the far field matches the surface pattern, the link between them can be mapped. Solar wind carries the field outward as it flows. Knowing that shape helps explain storms that reach Earth. Ness and Wilcox give an early, data-based picture of the field filling the space between Sun and Earth.
nasa-tm-19690000964-atlas-centaur-ac-12-:
Lewis Research Center evaluates the Atlas-Centaur AC-12 flight in this November 1968 memorandum. AC-12 launched on April 17, 1967, as the third operational Centaur flight. It carried Surveyor III toward the Moon on a lunar-intercept trajectory.

The ascent used parking-orbit mode. The Centaur first entered a circular orbit, then coasted under low-gravity conditions. From there it boosted the Surveyor spacecraft toward its lunar intercept path. Flight performance reports like this one check each vehicle system against predictions. They confirm the launch vehicle did its job for the lunar probe. Surveyor missions scouted the Moon ahead of crewed Apollo landings.
nasa-tm-19690003845-lighting-in-cryogeni:
Robert C. Hendricks and Kenneth J. Baumeister of Lewis Research Center show how to light fluids from inside in this report. Flow and heat-transfer studies often need illumination for visual observation and photography. The team submerged standard light bulbs in ordinary and cryogenic fluids to find safe operating conditions.

Successful operation happened whenever the bulb reached thermal equilibrium with its surroundings. A submerged bulb removes the need for a separate observation window. Windows bring leakage and lighting problems of their own. Internal bulbs can also provide localized heating along with light. A technical film supplement accompanied the report for readers who wanted motion pictures of the tests.
nasa-tm-19700024868-apollo-entry-summary:
James O. Rippey of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this document on March 17, 1969. It is the Apollo entry summary for Mission F, flown with vehicle AS-505. Mission F was Apollo 10, the final rehearsal before the first landing attempt.

The summary gathers the entry information crews and planners needed in one place. Entry is the fiery return through Earth's air at the end of a mission. The document served flight planning, crew training, and the making of onboard data files. It stands as a final copy, kept as a library record at the Houston center.
nasa-tm-19720005939-a-method-for-star-ve:
S W Crigler of TRW Systems Group and T J Blucker of the Manned Spacecraft Center wrote this internal note on June 30, 1971. Blucker worked in the Mathematical Physics Branch in Houston. The note, MSC-04446, supports Project Apollo. It gives a method for turning telescope sightings into a star direction. Apollo navigators fixed their craft's attitude by sighting known stars.

The crew used the alignment optical telescope in the lunar module. Each sighting produced a spiral reading, a cursor reading, and a time. The method converts those three values into the measured star vector. The vector comes out in lunar module body coordinates. Guidance computers could then compare it with the expected star position.
nasa-tm-19720009626-determination-of-atm:
R. H. Lang and P. O. Minott wrote this NASA preprint in November 1971, numbered X-524-71-470, on measuring atmospheric turbulence with a single laser receiver. Turbulence bends and blurs light crossing the air, which limits telescope performance. The wave structure function is the measure that captures how strong that distortion is.

Earlier measurement schemes needed two optical systems and two detectors, gear many laboratories did not have. Lang and Minott describe and analyze a method using the single-beam laser receiver instead. The procedure masks the telescope aperture with an opaque screen pierced by two small holes. Covering one hole, then comparing the readings, lets the lone detector extract the structure function.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
Volume one, number one of the New York Times Current History covers the European War from its start to March 1915. The Times Company published the monthly magazine in New York in 1915, with an index. Its first listed piece is by George Bernard Shaw.

Shaw's Common Sense About the War draws a storm of replies in the same number. Arnold Bennett calls it nonsense about Belgium, then states the German case. Cunninghame Graham picks at flaws in Shaw's logic, and Christabel Pankhurst calls him empty of good sense. Shaw also prints an open letter to President Wilson. The number shows a paper war fought beside the real one.
the-evolution-of-theology-an-anthropolog: Huxley traces gods back to ghosts: how early men made spirits, then gods, then God. Bold and closely argued, it brought science to religion's roots. A landmark of free thought, a landmark of free thought.
tom-swift-in-the-land-of-wonders-or-the-: Victor Appleton's Tom Swift (1917) sends the boy inventor underground. Inventions save the day repeatedly. The Tower library holds the full text. It thrilled young readers immensely. Science solves every peril neatly. Tom's pluck never fails him. The series inspired future engineers.
